summary: Defines the SIP Join header, which logically joins an existing SIP dialog with a new one. It enables features such as barge-in, message screening and call center monitoring.

eli5.summary: It lets a new person jump into an ongoing call, like a manager who quietly joins a support call.

questions: what is the sip join header
how does sip barge in work
what does 481 mean for a join request
subtitle: A SIP header that lets a new caller join an ongoing call without a central controller.

tldr.problem: Adding a new participant to an existing call normally needs a central controller (3pcc), or knowing a conference URI that may not even exist yet.
tldr.mechanism: The new party sends an INVITE with a Join header naming the Call-ID, to-tag and from-tag of the target dialog. The receiving user agent matches the dialog, checks authorization, and mixes or moves the call into a conference.
tldr.outcome: It enables peer-to-peer features such as barge-in, message screening and call center monitoring. Because it can expose a conversation, a join MUST only be accepted from an authenticated and authorized peer.

facts.label: Required parameters
facts.value: exactly one to-tag and one from-tag

today: RFC 3911 is a Proposed Standard, published in October 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Joining an Existing Dialog
sections.content:
The Join header logically joins an existing SIP dialog with a new one. It is part of the SIP multiparty applications framework and is especially useful in peer-to-peer call control, where a central controller (as in third-party call control, RFC 3725) may not be desirable.

An explicit Join is needed instead of just sending an INVITE to a conference URI because a conference may not exist yet (the target may be an ordinary two-party call), the joiner may not know the dialog is part of a conference, or it may not know the conference URI.

In the RFC's example, a Boss is talking to a Customer and asks an Assistant, out of band, to join. The Assistant gets the dialog information from somewhere such as a web page or an instant message, and sends the Boss an INVITE with a Join header. The Boss then mixes the media locally. This effectively creates a new conference, so the Boss generates a conference URI, returns it as the Contact of the Join INVITE (with the isfocus parameter), and re-INVITEs or UPDATEs the Customer with it.
sections.eli5: A boss is chatting with a customer. The boss tells an assistant which call it is, and the assistant dials in so all three can talk together.

sections.title: Why This Is Not a Wiretap
sections.content:
Join can build monitoring services, so the RFC checks it against the definition of wiretapping in RFC 2804. That definition has four conditions. Item 2, that none of the recipient parties know about the delivery to the third party, does not apply here: one party is always aware of a Join request and can decline it.

The RFC adds that in many uses some or all of the other items may not apply either. For example, many call centers that handle financial transactions record all conversations with the full knowledge and expectation of everyone involved.
sections.eli5: Someone listening in secretly is a wiretap. Here the person being joined always gets asked and can say no, so it is not sneaky.

sections.title: How the Receiver Handles a Join
sections.content:
The Join header holds the information needed to match a dialog: Call-ID, to-tag and from-tag. The receiving UA tries to match it against a confirmed or early dialog, comparing the to-tag with the local tag and the from-tag with the remote tag, as if they were tags in an incoming request.

The UAS MUST reject with 400 Bad Request if there is more than one Join header, if Join appears in a request other than INVITE, or if a header with contradictory semantics (for example Replaces) is also present. If Join matches more than one dialog, the UA MUST act as if no match was found. With no match, but a Request-URI that is a conference URI, the UAS MUST ignore the Join and process the INVITE normally. Otherwise no match gets 481, as does a match on a dialog not created with an INVITE. A match on an already terminated dialog SHOULD be declined with 603.

For an active dialog, the UA MUST verify that the initiator is authorized. That holds if the initiator authenticated as equivalent to the user being joined, for example by sharing Digest credentials or by signing with S/MIME using the same private key and certificate. A Referred-By header that corresponds to the joined user, backed by a valid Referred-By Authenticated Identity Body (RFC 3893), should be treated as authorized. The UA may also keep a list of authorized entities or apply local policy.

If authorized, the UA tries to accept the INVITE and assign mixing resources. If it cannot (for example, incompatible media), it MUST return an error and MUST leave the matched dialog unchanged. If it lacks local resources, it SHOULD create a conference on a resource such as a conference server and redirect the requestor and other participants there, using only mechanisms they are expected to accept. If it is incapable of satisfying the join, it MUST return 488 Not Acceptable Here.
sections.eli5: The person getting the request looks for the call with that name tag. If there is no such call, or the asker is not allowed in, the answer is no. If all is fine, they make room and mix everyone's voices together.

sections.title: Sender and Proxy Behavior
sections.content:
A UAC that wants to add its own dialog to an existing early or confirmed dialog MAY send an INVITE with a Join header carrying the target's Call-ID, to-tag and from-tag. If it receives a 300-class response and sends the INVITE on to a Contact, that redirected INVITE MUST carry the same Join header. Join cannot match multiple dialogs, an entire call or a transaction, and it cannot follow a chain of proxy forking.

Proxies need no new behavior and pass the header transparently. The RFC notes that a proxy that forks on application logic, such as caller screening or time-of-day routing, might send the INVITE to a completely different set of Contacts, in which case the Join INVITE will fail.
sections.eli5: The person asking just includes the call's name tag. The messengers in the middle pass the note along without opening it.

sections.title: Syntax and the join Option Tag
sections.content:
Join is a request header, defined only for INVITE requests, and it MAY be encrypted as part of end-to-end encryption. Only one Join value may appear in a request. It MUST contain exactly one to-tag and exactly one from-tag. For compatibility with dialogs from RFC 2543 user agents, a tag of zero matches both a value of zero and a null tag.

The RFC also defines the option tag join. UAs that support Join MUST put it in a Supported header. UAs that want explicit failure if Join is unsupported MAY put it in a Require header, for example Require: join, 100rel.
sections.eli5: The header always has the call's ID plus two little name tags, one for each side, so exactly one call can be found.

sections.title: Usage Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two non-normative scenarios. In the first, the join is accepted and the call is moved to a central conference. A sends B an INVITE with a Join header for B's call with C. B does not mix locally. It INVITEs a conference server, redirects A to the conference with a 302, and REFERs C to the conference as well, then ends its own dialog with C. The conference server mixes the three sessions together, and the result looks identical to the locally mixed case, with the details transparent to A.

In the second example, the join is rejected. B is busy and does not want to be disturbed, so it answers A's INVITE with 486 Busy. The RFC notes B could also have declined with a 603. The examples are ideas only, not an exhaustive list of uses.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the boss hands everyone over to a bigger meeting room instead of mixing the voices alone, and the newcomer never needs to know how it was done.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension significantly changes the relative security of SIP devices. Today, even if an eavesdropper learns the Call-ID, To and From of a dialog, they cannot easily modify or destroy it when Digest authentication or end-to-end message integrity are used. Join can be used to insert or monitor sensitive content in a conversation.

Join invitations MUST therefore only be accepted if the requester has been properly authenticated by a standard SIP mechanism (Digest or S/MIME) and is authorized to join the target dialog. Authorization is generally configured as local policy over long-lived relationships: for example, call center agents' UAs may carry a list of supervisors and monitoring agents allowed to join, or rely on a shorter list of authorized hosts such as a certificate authority.

The dialog information (Call-ID, to-tag, from-tag) may be learned from URIs on a web page, event package subscriptions or REFER notifications. Using end-to-end security to integrity protect and encrypt it is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Letting someone join your call is powerful, so you only let in people you have checked and trust, like a call center that keeps a list of supervisors.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC registers a new SIP header, Join, which has no short form and is normatively described in the syntax section of this document. It also registers a new SIP option tag, join, described as support for the SIP Join header, with Join as the SIP header it defines.
sections.eli5: The RFC asks to put the new header and its option tag on the official list so nobody else uses the same names.

messages.label: INVITE + Join
messages.note: Join names the Boss and Customer dialog (Call-ID 7@c).

messages.label: reINVITE
messages.note: Moves the Customer to the new conference URI.

viz.caption: RESPONSES A UAS RETURNS FOR A JOIN REQUEST

items.label: Bad Request
items.desc: More than one Join, Join in a non-INVITE, or a contradictory header such as Replaces.

items.label: Call/Transaction Does Not Exist
items.desc: No matching dialog, or the match was not created with an INVITE.

items.label: Declined
items.desc: The matched dialog has already terminated (SHOULD).

items.label: Not Acceptable Here
items.desc: The UAS is incapable of satisfying the Join request.

viz.caption: JOIN HEADER ABNF AND EXAMPLE (FROM RFC 3911)

data.title: Join header syntax
data.code:
Join            = "Join" HCOLON callid *(SEMI join-param)
join-param      = to-tag / from-tag / generic-param
to-tag          = "to-tag" EQUAL token
from-tag        = "from-tag" EQUAL token

Join: 12adf2f34456gs5;to-tag=12345;from-tag=54321
